facts.claim: Smartraveller's overall advice for Türkiye is 'Exercise a high degree of caution' (Level 2) due to the threat of terrorism; higher levels apply in some areas. Page updated 30 October 2026, still current at 2 November 2026.

Smartraveller: Do not travel (Level 4) within 10km of the border with Syria; Reconsider your need to travel (Level 3) to Hakkari and Şırnak provinces, including the Esendere border crossing in Hakkari.
Smartraveller: Türkiye does not legally recognise same-sex marriages, civil unions or domestic partnerships.

A Turkish municipal marriage office (evlendirme dairesi) handles marriage applications: Beyoğlu Municipality in Istanbul lists its own Beyoğlu Evlendirme Dairesi and the documents it requires for foreign nationals (example of one municipality; requirements can differ by office).

Beyoğlu Municipality lists for foreign nationals: 3 passport photos taken within the last six months; a health report showing no impediment to the marriage (from a family physician or state hospital, or a private one approved by a family physician); a Marriage Eligibility Certificate or Certificate of Celibacy; and a notarised translation of the passport or photo ID.

Beyoğlu Municipality: the Marriage Eligibility Certificate or Certificate of Celibacy obtained from the person's own consulate must be certified (apostilled) at a district governorate office; if the consulate is in Ankara, it is certified by the Turkish Ministry of Foreign Affairs; if brought from the home country, it must be certified by the Turkish Embassy or apostilled. If it does not show the parents' names, a birth certificate is required.

Beyoğlu Municipality: the couple must attend the application together on weekdays (09:00 to 12:00 and 13:00 to 16:30), or appoint a proxy with a specific photo power of attorney; incomplete applications are not accepted. No fee is stated on the page.

Smartraveller (updated 18 August 2026): some countries ask you to prove you are free to marry; the most common documents are a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) and certificates from a registry of births, deaths and marriages. DFAT can issue a CNI in Australia, but some local authorities only accept CNIs issued in their country; ask the destination's embassy whether you need a CNI, where to get it and whether it needs an authentication or apostille.

Smartraveller: you can't register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if it was valid under the law of the country where it happened and would have been valid under Australian law; a foreign marriage certificate is usually accepted as proof, though it may not work as proof of a name change. Talk to a lawyer to confirm validity.
Smartraveller: Australia doesn't recognise overseas marriages where a party is already married, not old enough, too closely related, or forced to marry.

Gelin alma (also gelin göçü or gelin göçürme) is the taking of the bride from her father's house to the groom's family home, by a party called the gelin alayı that sets out from the groom's house; davul and zurna accompany the departure, with dancing along the way, and the music also announces the wedding. (Alpyıldız, E. 2020, 'Evlenme Geçiş Dönemi Geleneğine Müzik Davranışları Açısından Bakış: Gelin Ağlatma-Alma-İndirme Havaları Örneği', KSBD 12(22): 267-277; author at Hacettepe University, Department of Turkish Folklore; read via SciSpace PDF copy)

When the gelin alayı reaches the bride's home the music changes to slower 'gelin alma' or 'gelin çıkarma' melodies, usually instrumental, with davul as the rhythm instrument and zurna or clarinet as the wind instrument, marking her farewell to her family home. (Alpyıldız, E. 2020, 'Evlenme Geçiş Dönemi Geleneğine Müzik Davranışları Açısından Bakış: Gelin Ağlatma-Alma-İndirme Havaları Örneği', KSBD 12(22): 267-277; author at Hacettepe University, Department of Turkish Folklore; read via SciSpace PDF copy)

Bayrak asma (raising the flag) is described as the symbolic announcement that the wedding has begun, a flag raised at the wedding house with davul and zurna played as it goes up. (Alpyıldız, E. 2020, 'Evlenme Geçiş Dönemi Geleneğine Müzik Davranışları Açısından Bakış: Gelin Ağlatma-Alma-İndirme Havaları Örneği', KSBD 12(22): 267-277; author at Hacettepe University, Department of Turkish Folklore; read via SciSpace PDF copy)

Davul and zurna are described as the symbol that a wedding is taking place, their sound carrying over wide areas; a proverb runs 'Düğünde davul zurna, hamamda kurna' (davul and zurna at a wedding, the basin at a bathhouse). (Alpyıldız, E. 2020, 'Evlenme Geçiş Dönemi Geleneğine Müzik Davranışları Açısından Bakış: Gelin Ağlatma-Alma-İndirme Havaları Örneği', KSBD 12(22): 267-277; author at Hacettepe University, Department of Turkish Folklore; read via SciSpace PDF copy)

On arrival at the groom's home, gift rituals (under names such as indirmelik) to persuade the bride to step down from the horse or car are seen in almost every region; drummers may also playfully block the way for a tip. (Alpyıldız, E. 2020, 'Evlenme Geçiş Dönemi Geleneğine Müzik Davranışları Açısından Bakış: Gelin Ağlatma-Alma-İndirme Havaları Örneği', KSBD 12(22): 267-277; author at Hacettepe University, Department of Turkish Folklore; read via SciSpace PDF copy)

Today the kına gecesi is also held in new urban forms, functioning partly like a hen's party (bekarlığa veda), with changes in dress, music, food and venue. (Alpyıldız, E. 2020, 'Evlenme Geçiş Dönemi Geleneğine Müzik Davranışları Açısından Bakış: Gelin Ağlatma-Alma-İndirme Havaları Örneği', KSBD 12(22): 267-277; author at Hacettepe University, Department of Turkish Folklore; read via SciSpace PDF copy)

SEARCH-SUMMARY-ONLY (full text not read): Sibel Turhan Tuna, 'Türk Dünyasındaki Düğünlerde Koltuklama ve Kırmızı Kuşak Bağlama Geleneği', Bilig 38 (2006): 149ff, a folklore study of the tradition of tying a red sash (kırmızı kuşak bağlama) on the bride, described in the indexed abstract as still practised in various Turkish provinces. Search snippets indicate the paper links it to guardianship passing from the bride's father; not confirmed from the full text.
facts.conflicts: Old Wedded Wonderland page framed the sash as 'purity'; the academic abstract read via search summary does not confirm that framing. Who ties it (father or brother) not confirmed.

insider_details.detail: For Australians the legal wedding in Türkiye is the civil one at the municipal marriage office, so plan the documents first: the Beyoğlu office in Istanbul, for example, asks foreign nationals for a marriage eligibility certificate or certificate of celibacy that has been apostilled or certified, a Turkish health report and a notarised passport translation. Treat that list as one office's version and confirm with the office you book.

Build the paperwork timeline from Australia backwards: Smartraveller says DFAT can issue a CNI in Australia, but some local authorities only accept ones issued in-country, and the Beyoğlu page expects the certificate from the person's own consulate, so ask the marriage office and the embassy which version they accept before anyone flies.

Both partners usually need to front up together on a weekday to lodge the application (Beyoğlu lists 09:00 to 12:00 and 13:00 to 16:30), so schedule an arrival buffer of working days before the ceremony date rather than landing the day before.

If you want davul and zurna for an arrival or gelin alma moment, think of them as outdoor instruments: the folklore literature describes them as the sound that announces a wedding across wide areas, so check the venue's music rules and neighbours before booking them indoors or late.

Keep the venue outside Smartraveller's higher-level areas (within 10km of the Syrian border, Hakkari and Şırnak) and recheck the page before booking, because levels change; it was updated 30 October 2026.
Same-sex couples cannot have a legally recognised marriage in Türkiye (Smartraveller), so the Wedded Advisor would plan a celebration there with the legal marriage done elsewhere.
